mstts:express-as.prosody:
Welcome to this journey, where we peel back the layers of power, influence, and the endless pursuit of security that have shaped the world as we know it. But what if there’s something deeper beneath the headlines—a real struggle over where our global order is headed? Together, we're about to explore questions that don’t just linger on the surface, but cut right to the heart of what kind of world we want to live in. Noam Chomsky’s powerful work, Hegemony or Survival: America's Quest for Global Dominance, takes us behind the scenes of U.S. foreign policy, urging us to look closely at the motivations and ripple effects of a superpower’s relentless reach. As we dive in, you'll notice how the clash between national interests and the greater good of humanity isn’t just a distant debate—it’s a question that touches all of us. What happens when military might and unilateral decisions shape the world’s future? Can unchecked power really bring security, or does it threaten the very foundation of peace and cooperation?
Step by step, we’ll unravel the web of political, economic, and military moves that have defined decades of international relations. We’ll see how official words often hide covert actions, and how, even in the face of overwhelming power, voices of dissent and hope still push back, fighting for justice and the right to self-determination.
So, as we move forward together, let’s stay curious, open-minded, and ready to question the paths that lead either toward lasting security—or the risk of endless conflict. The choices we examine here don’t just shape nations—they help decide the future of our entire planet.

Chapter One: The Pursuit of Power Over Shared Security.
Picture this—you’re sitting around a kitchen table with a few close friends, sharing stories and worries as the world outside feels like it’s spinning faster every day.
Someone, the history buff of the group, leans in and wonders, “Why do some countries act like the whole world is theirs to control?”
Before you know it, the conversation lands on the United States—a country that’s shaped global events in more ways than most of us realize.
And it leads to a big question: What really happens when a single nation decides its own interests matter more than everyone else’s?
Let’s take a closer look at how the U.S. has chased global dominance.
After World War Two, the world was in shambles. The United States stood almost alone, with unmatched economic and military power.
The temptation to use that power to shape the future? It was huge.
But instead of joining others to create a safer, more cooperative world, the U.S. often chose to go it alone—setting its own rules and expecting everyone to follow.
Over the years, this became a habit. When a crisis hit—be it Latin America, the Middle East, or Southeast Asia—American leaders started viewing the world like a chessboard, shifting pieces to protect their own interests.
They used words like “democracy” and “freedom” to justify these moves.
But on the ground, things were rarely that simple. Real people, in faraway places, ended up caught between their own struggles and the ambitions of a distant superpower.
Here’s a story that really brings it home.
Imagine a small town in Central America, where families are just trying to rebuild after years of conflict. They dream of peace, but instead, they’re forced to live in fear. Outside forces come in, arming and training local militias—all under the banner of fighting communism.
Suddenly, their daily lives are shaped by decisions made thousands of miles away, in rooms filled with maps and strategies. The promise of democracy? It doesn’t mean much when it shows up at the end of a rifle.
And back in the U.S., most folks never see this side of the story. The news is full of official statements and patriotic images, but rarely the human cost.
That gap—the one between the language of freedom and the reality of violence—just keeps growing with each new conflict.
It becomes clear that chasing dominance isn’t just about security. It’s about holding onto power—no questions asked.
But here’s something to pay attention to: Acting alone, the U.S. often undermined international agreements and organizations that were supposed to keep the peace.
The United Nations, which was meant to give every nation a voice, got pushed aside whenever it clashed with American interests.
International law? It was used when convenient, ignored when it wasn’t.
And these choices didn’t just affect distant countries.
At home, the focus on military strength and overseas threats shaped what people cared about—and what the government spent money on.
Resources that could’ve gone to things like education, health care, or fighting poverty were instead funneled into weapons and foreign operations.
The idea that safety only comes through dominance became a self-fulfilling prophecy—making everyone, in the end, a bit less safe.
As the friends around that kitchen table wrap up their talk, one of them asks, “Isn’t there a better way? Couldn’t we choose cooperation over control, shared security over going it alone?”
The question lingers, hanging in the air, as the world keeps trying to make sense of the choices made in the name of power.

Chapter 2. The Hidden Costs of Intervention.
Picture a quiet neighborhood. There’s a teacher, prepping her lessons on world history, trying to help her students make sense of the forces that really shape their lives. She knows the textbooks tend to smooth over the rough edges—wars and interventions are often painted as steps toward progress. But deep down, she understands there’s so much more to the story. Behind every headline, there are real people whose lives are turned upside down by decisions made far away.
If you look closely at recent history, you’ll notice a pattern—one where U.S. intervention abroad shows up again and again. American leaders have often justified military action by saying it’s all about protecting freedom, stopping dangerous ideologies, or defending national interests. But if you’re living in the middle of it all, things are rarely so simple.
Imagine a family in Southeast Asia during the Vietnam War. Their village—once just a peaceful place—suddenly becomes a battleground. Foreign troops show up, promising liberation, but what really arrives is destruction. The parents do everything they can to keep their kids safe, dodging landmines and holding onto hope in a world that feels so uncertain. The war, sold as a fight for democracy, ends up leaving scars that last for generations.
Or think about a young doctor in the Middle East, working in a city torn apart by conflict. Every day, she sees the true cost of airstrikes and sanctions—kids suffering from malnutrition, elders unable to get the medicine they need. The official explanations for these hardships never quite match what she witnesses firsthand. All that talk of humanitarian intervention? For her patients, it rings painfully hollow when basic needs go unmet.
And these stories—they’re not just one-offs. From Central America to the Persian Gulf, the pattern repeats itself: interventions justified by noble goals, but the real outcome is often chaos, displacement, and a deep, lingering instability. The folks who feel it the most? They’re usually the ones with the least say in how things unfold.
Back in the U.S., most people’s understanding of these events comes from official statements and a steady stream of media coverage. The spotlight is usually on military strategy or whether an operation succeeded—not on the human cost. And when mistakes are admitted, they’re often explained away as unfortunate, but necessary, sacrifices for a supposed greater good.
Over time, the impact of all these interventions adds up. Instead of building stability, they often plant the seeds for future conflict. When governments collapse, new armed groups fill the vacuum, and resentment toward foreign interference just keeps growing. It’s a cycle of violence that rarely ends, all driven by the idea that might makes right.
The teacher, thinking about all this, can’t help but wonder—what if the voices of those most affected were actually heard? What if the people making these decisions listened to the stories of families caught in the crossfire? Would anything change? It’s a question that hangs in the air, especially as new crises keep popping up, and those old habits of intervention just won’t go away.

Chapter 3: Media Narratives and the Shaping of Public Perception
Picture this—a journalist at her desk, surrounded by stacks of reports from around the world. She’s passionate about telling stories that truly matter, but the reality is... deadlines loom, and there’s always that pressure from editors about what’s “newsworthy.” The clock’s ticking, and she barely has time to scratch beneath the surface before the next story demands her attention.
Most of what we see on the news? It’s been filtered—sometimes heavily—through official statements, press releases, and carefully crafted narratives. Stories don’t just land on our screens by accident. There’s a whole process behind the scenes, shaping what ends up in front of us.
This is where the media can quietly become a partner in the quest for dominance. Think about it: when a government launches a military campaign, or tries to justify a controversial policy, the press is often expected to pass along the official line. If reporters push back—if they ask too many tough questions—they risk losing access, or worse, being branded as unpatriotic. So what do we get? A steady stream of coverage that frames events in ways that support those in power.
And during a crisis, this pattern only gets stronger. After a major attack or some international incident, everyone wants answers—and fast. News outlets jump into action, but they lean heavily on government sources. Suddenly, the language shifts. It’s all about national security, unity, and standing together. Dissenting voices? They’re drowned out, replaced by simple stories of good versus evil, us versus them.
Now, if you’re sitting at home, flipping on the evening news, it’s tough to see past the surface. The images are powerful—flags waving, leaders speaking solemnly, troops heading off to distant places. The focus is on heroism, on sacrifice. But we rarely hear about the messy realities of war, or what happens long after the cameras leave. And those who dare to question whether these actions are wise? Their voices hardly make it into the story.
Every so often, something breaks through. Maybe a whistleblower steps forward, revealing abuses that were hidden from view. Or a determined reporter uncovers evidence of civilian casualties. In those moments, we’re forced to confront the gap between what we’re told and what’s actually happening. But honestly, those moments are fleeting. The news cycle moves on, and those uncomfortable truths? They’re quickly forgotten.
Imagine that same journalist, frustrated by the limits of her job, wondering what might happen if the media really embraced its role as a watchdog. What if reporters consistently challenged official narratives, and made space for the perspectives of people most affected by these decisions? Maybe then, the public would demand more accountability. But as long as the flow of information is tightly controlled by people in power, it’s tough to break the cycle. The pattern of complicity just keeps repeating.

Chapter 4: Undermining International Law and Global Institutions
Imagine this: In a bustling city, there’s a law student hunched over her desk, surrounded by heavy casebooks about the United Nations and all the rules that are supposed to keep countries in check. She’s genuinely drawn to the idea that nations can actually solve tough problems peacefully—through conversation and compromise, not threats or force.
But the more she reads, the more she spots something troubling. The rules? They’re often twisted, or just flat-out ignored—especially by the countries holding the most power.
Now, let’s talk about the United States. With its vast resources and global influence, America’s played a huge role in shaping how the world works together. But here’s the catch: whenever international law gets in the way of its goals, the U.S. often just... makes its own path. Treaties are signed, then dropped. Agreements are made, then broken. The unspoken message? The rules are for everyone else—not for those who set them.
One example really sticks with our law student. Not long ago, the United Nations Security Council refused to approve military action in a major conflict. But the U.S. and its allies pushed ahead anyway, insisting their cause was just. That decision set off outrage around the globe. Other nations saw it as a dangerously slippery slope. After all, if the world’s most powerful country can ignore the rules, what’s to stop anyone else from doing the same?
And this isn’t just a recent issue—it’s been happening for decades. Throughout the postwar era, the U.S. has used its influence to steer the international system in its favor. When global institutions line up with American interests, they get praise and funding. But the moment they push back, they’re brushed aside as irrelevant or even obstructive.
The end result? We’ve got a world order that’s both strong and fragile. Sure, it can accomplish amazing things, but it’s also vulnerable—especially when those with the most power decide to change the rules on a whim.
Now, think about what this means for smaller countries. Without the protection of international law, they’re left to fend for themselves, navigating a world where might often wins out over what’s right. All those efforts to build a more just and fair global system? They get undermined by the reality of power politics. The whole idea of collective security starts to sound a little empty when the rules themselves can shift overnight.
So, as our law student looks back on everything she’s learned, she can’t help but wonder—what would it actually take to create a system where every nation truly stands equal before the law? She dreams of a world where cooperation and respect replace the old logic of dominance.
But as long as the most powerful countries reserve the right to go it alone, that dream of a fair and peaceful international order stays just out of reach.

Chapter 5: The Threat to Democracy at Home and Abroad
Picture this: a community organizer stands at the front of a local hall, facing a small crowd. She’s talking about why democracy matters—our right to vote, the need for open debate, and how important it is to hold our leaders accountable.
But as she scans the faces in the room, she senses something—cynicism. Folks have seen just how fragile democracy can be. Not just close to home, but in places far away, too.
You see, when a country is always chasing global dominance, it doesn’t just reshape foreign policy—it echoes back into everyday life. The constant drumbeat of security and the fear of outside threats can create a climate of suspicion. And that’s where it gets dangerous. In the name of safety, civil liberties start to slip away. Genuine dissent? Suddenly, it’s painted as disloyalty. The space for honest debate shrinks, and what you can safely say gets squeezed tighter and tighter.
Now, let’s look beyond our own borders. In other countries, the effects can be even more stark. When the U.S. backs authoritarian regimes or tries to steer elections, it betrays the very promise of democracy. People who risk it all—demanding freedom and justice—find themselves trapped. On one side, local crackdowns. On the other, foreign interference, both claiming to stand for democracy but often acting out of self-interest.
There’s one story that sticks with the organizer: a group of students in a distant country, meeting in secret to talk about their hopes. They dream of a place where everyone has a voice, where leaders answer to the people, and the law protects everyone equally. But instead, they’re met with threats and violence—sometimes even from foreign powers who say they support democracy, but whose actions tell a different story.
So, back in that local hall, the organizer urges everyone not to lose hope. She reminds them: democracy isn’t just handed down from above. It’s something we have to build, and protect, every single day. The fight for real self-government never really ends, and every decision by those in power sends ripples across the globe.
As the meeting wraps up, the crowd drifts out, each person feeling the weight of these challenges. The road to a more just and democratic world isn’t easy, and it’s never certain—but the hope for change is still alive.
And there’s a question we all have to ask: will the drive for dominance keep chipping away at the values we claim to defend? Or—could we finally see a new commitment to cooperation and accountability take root?

Chapter 6: The Logic of Preventive War
You know, there’s a certain tension that fills the air when people start talking about the future—especially when the topic shifts to threats that haven’t even happened yet.
Picture a typical suburban living room: neighbors gathered for a potluck, sharing food and small talk. Suddenly, the conversation drifts to the latest headlines—rumors about dangers far away, and warnings about weapons that might, one day, be aimed at them. You can almost feel the unease settle in, even though nothing’s actually happened.
It’s in moments like these that the idea of preventive war starts to make sense to some folks. The logic is tempting: if there’s a chance a threat might emerge, why not act now, before it becomes real? For decision-makers in Washington, this way of thinking offers a powerful justification—military action, not just as a reaction, but as a way to stop trouble before it starts. On paper, it sounds like prudence, a strategy to keep the country safe in an unpredictable world.
But let’s flip the perspective. Imagine waking up in a city halfway across the globe—suddenly, your world is shaken by explosions. Your government’s been accused of dangerous ambitions, and now your life is upended by a war you never chose. The attack isn’t based on solid proof. It’s sparked by suspicion and what-ifs.
As the dust settles, something becomes clear: the logic behind preventive war is a slippery slope. Once you lower the bar for military action—once “maybe” becomes enough—it gets a whole lot easier to justify the next intervention. Instead of making the world safer, things get more unstable. Countries start scrambling to protect themselves, afraid they’ll be the next target. It’s a cycle—fear leads to violence, which sparks even more fear, making true security feel further and further away.
Back at that potluck, the neighbors can’t help but wonder—is there a better way to deal with all this uncertainty? Could trust and cooperation ever replace force and suspicion? That question hangs in the air, unanswered, as the world wrestles with the aftermath of a strategy that promises safety, but all too often, delivers only more insecurity.

Chapter Seven: The Environmental Costs of Empire
Picture this—a park ranger, starting her morning by walking the quiet trails of a national forest. She breathes in the fresh air and takes in the beauty all around her. But she can’t help but think about something bigger: how the health of this forest, and the planet as a whole, is shaped by choices made not just here, but all over the world.
As she flips through reports about military exercises, oil drilling, and the spread of bases across continents, a troubling pattern jumps out. What’s the real price of global power? Turns out, it’s not just political or economic—it’s environmental, too.
Think about it: military operations use up enormous amounts of energy and resources. They leave behind pollution, tear down forests, and damage delicate ecosystems. Bases often end up in the most fragile places, and the heavy machinery of war leaves marks that can last for generations. The real kicker? These costs are often hidden, felt most by communities far from those making the decisions.
Imagine a coastal village where fishermen notice their daily catch is shrinking. The once-clear waters are now cloudy with runoff from a nearby base. The constant noise and activity have thrown the sea’s natural rhythms out of balance. For these villagers, whose way of life has been passed down for generations, everything is at risk—all because of choices made in distant capitals. Security for some ends up costing others their livelihoods—and the health of our planet.
The ranger can’t help but see the irony: the very policies meant to protect a nation’s future are actually chipping away at the foundations of life itself. Our environment—already strained by climate change and overuse—is pushed even closer to the edge by the demands of empire. And when you really look at it, the true cost of dominance isn’t just measured in money or lives lost. It’s in the loss of our irreplaceable natural heritage.
She finds herself wondering—what would it take to change course? What if we saw the world not as something to be controlled, but as a shared home that needs our care? Maybe the answer starts with recognizing how deeply connected we all are—and choosing cooperation over conquest.

Chapter 8: The Dangers of Unchecked Power
Picture this—a bustling café, filled with the low hum of conversation. At one table, a group of university students leans in, deep in debate about what power really means. Some say you need strength to keep things in order. Others? They're nervous about what happens if anyone—or any nation—gets too much control.
Underneath their lively discussion, there's this shared worry: What if power ends up in just a few hands?
If you look back through history, you’ll see plenty of warnings. Every time checks and balances get pushed aside, it opens the door for abuse. Take U.S. foreign policy as an example. Over the years, more and more decisions about war and peace have landed squarely in the hands of the executive branch.
Congressional approval? Often ignored. And regular people—folks like you and me—are left in the dark about what these choices really cost, and what they actually mean.
There’s a story from a retired government official that really brings this home. They remember feeling pressure to just go along with decisions that seemed rushed, or honestly, barely justified. The machinery of government moves fast, and if you speak up, you risk getting pushed to the sidelines.
In that kind of system, loyalty to superiors is rewarded far more than careful, critical thinking. Caution? It gets treated like a weakness, not a strength.
But here’s the thing—these aren’t just problems for people inside government. When transparency and accountability start to slip away, everyone feels it, even if it’s subtle.
Think about it: When leaders don’t answer for their actions, it becomes harder for ordinary citizens to hold them to account. Over time, that feeling of having a voice in your own democracy begins to fade, replaced by resignation, or even cynicism.
Back in that café, the students start to realize something important: Unchecked power isn’t just an idea you read about in textbooks. It shapes the world they walk through every day.
So what’s the answer? The challenge is to bring back real balance—to make sure decisions about war and peace happen out in the open, with honest debate and real input.
It’s not easy. It takes vigilance, courage, and the willingness to question even the things we think we know for sure.

Chapter 9: Resistance and the Power of Solidarity.
Picture this—a small apartment, a handful of activists huddled together, planning their next move. They come from all walks of life, but they've got one thing in common: this unshakable belief that ordinary people, people just like you and me, really can change the world—even when it feels like the odds are stacked sky-high against them.
Their conversations? They're electric, full of stories about resistance. Some are about entire communities rising up against injustice. Others are about that one person who simply refuses to stay silent. And you know what? It's these stories, these small sparks of courage, that have always been the starting point for big movements—movements for justice, for peace, for something better.
Imagine workers in a city, banding together to strike against unfair treatment, even when they're threatened by those in power. Or students staging a sit-in, putting everything on the line to demand an end to a war they know just isn't right. Most of these acts? They don't make the evening news. But they set something in motion, sending ripples that inspire others to step up and join in.
The activists in that apartment, they've learned a tough lesson: real change is never quick, and it's rarely easy. There are setbacks. There are days filled with disappointment. And let's be honest, the obstacles can feel overwhelming. But here's what keeps them going—solidarity. When people join hands, reach across borders, and come together despite their differences, that's when real power shows up. That's when even the oldest, most stubborn systems can be challenged.
One activist shares a memory—how a protest in their own city was suddenly joined by people from all over the world, all standing together for peace. That feeling? It was incredible. Suddenly, it was clear: this fight for justice, it isn't just happening here or now. It's everywhere, all the time.
As the meeting wraps up, everyone heads out feeling recharged, with a deeper sense of purpose. Sure, the road ahead is uncertain. But they've got something powerful on their side: the knowledge that none of them are in this alone. And that's the heart of it—the power of solidarity. It's what breaks through the logic of dominance, and reminds us all that, together, we really can make a difference.

Chapter Ten: Imagining a Different Future.
Picture this: it’s a quiet evening. A parent is tucking their child into bed, and the room is filled with those gentle, curious questions only kids can ask. The child wonders aloud—why is there so much conflict out there? Is the world always going to be this way? The parent pauses, searching for words that are both honest and hopeful.
You know, it’s so easy to feel overwhelmed by everything that’s happening in the world. Sometimes, the weight of old mistakes—years of dominance and intervention—can feel like they’ve left scars that will never heal. And if you’ve ever wondered where we go from here, you’re not alone. The road to a more just and peaceful future isn’t exactly marked out for us.
But here’s something you might not expect: history isn’t destiny. The actions we choose today can actually shape what tomorrow looks like.
All over the world, people are quietly working on new ways to live and work together. There are local projects popping up—conflict resolution circles, environmental cleanups, communities experimenting with more direct democracy. Maybe these efforts seem small, maybe even a bit fragile. But each one is a little glimpse into what’s possible. They show us a future built not on power or fear, but on cooperation, respect, and shared responsibility.
So, what does the parent say to their child? Change is possible. But it’s not easy—it takes imagination, and a little bit of courage. It means questioning the old ways of doing things, listening to people whose voices have been ignored, and building bridges where there used to be walls. It means realizing that real security doesn’t come from being the strongest, but from building justice and mutual respect.
As the child finally drifts off to sleep, the parent sits quietly, thinking about the power of hope. The truth is, the future isn’t written yet. And the chance for a better world? It’s still out there—if enough of us are willing to reach for it, and work together to make it real.

As we wrap up our journey through the ideas of “Hegemony or Survival,” let’s take a moment to bring it all together. If you’ve been following along, you’ve seen how the drive for dominance—even when it starts with good intentions—can set off waves of consequences that reach far beyond what we see in the news. The world isn’t just a chessboard, and real people are never just pieces to be moved around. These lessons aren’t just for leaders or experts—they’re for anyone who cares about the future we’re building, and the world we’ll leave behind.
So, what’s the key takeaway here? Unchecked power always risks fueling new cycles of violence and uncertainty. Headlines rarely capture the human cost of intervention. When we neglect international law and global institutions, they lose their strength. And let’s not forget—the environment pays a heavy price when military force takes center stage. In the end, real security grows from cooperation, justice, and the courage to imagine new ways forward.
Right now, the world stands at a crossroads. The habits of control and intervention run deep, but they aren’t set in stone. Every one of us can choose to listen more closely, to question what we’re told, and to act with empathy. Building a more just and peaceful world won’t happen overnight—but every conversation, every act of solidarity, and every effort to hold power accountable gets us a little closer.
And if the scale of it all feels overwhelming, remember—change often starts with something small. It might be a question you ask, a story you share, or simply reaching out to someone in friendship. The future isn’t locked in place. By choosing cooperation over control, and hope over fear, you can help shape a world where survival isn’t a privilege for the few, but a right for all.
